## Claims

### C-R4-001
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo holds that James 1:19–2:26 is the only larger section with fairly obvious conceptual unity (true religion / works the word requires); the following paragraphs (3:1–4:12) are not bound by a single continuous theme, though they stand in a loose relationship.
- **quote:** "James 1:19-2:26 is the only larger section of the letter that has a fairly obvious conceptual unity… No such theme binds together the following paragraphs… while James is obviously not consistently elaborating a single theme, two considerations suggest that these paragraphs are joined in a loose relationship."
- **locus:** L6
- **passage:** Intro to 3:1–4:12

### C-R4-002
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo’s two grounds for loose unity of 3:1–4:12: (1) the unit opens (3:1–12) and closes (4:11–12) with warnings about misuse of speech in community; (2) the topics co-occur in secular and Jewish moral exhortation.
- **quote:** "First, the passage begins (3:1-12) and ends (4:11-12) with warnings about the misuse of speech, especially in the context of the community… Second, the topics that James treats in these paragraphs are also sometimes found together in both secular and Jewish moral exhortation."
- **locus:** L6
- **passage:** Intro to 3:1–4:12

### C-R4-003
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo, citing Johnson, links 3:13–4:10 to the ancient topos “On jealousy,” which often traced violent behavior (4:1–3) to jealousy; similar exhortations can include rebukes of sinful speech (e.g. T. Gad 4–5); James brings “quarreling” into the center of this moral topos (4:1).
- **quote:** "Johnson has demonstrated the similarity of 3:13-4:10 to the ancient topos (\"topical discussion\") \"On jealousy,\" which often traced violent behavior (4:1-3) to jealousy… James himself brings \"quarreling\" right into the center of his appropriation of this popular moral topos (4:1)."
- **locus:** L6
- **passage:** Intro; Johnson topos “On jealousy”

### C-R4-004
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo identifies the heart of James’s concern in this section as violent quarrels shaking the community; material can be loosely related to that concern, but he rejects a genuine chiasm for 3:1–4:12 (only superficial contact between 3:13–18 and 4:4–10); 4:4–10 is a critical, letter-wide call to repentance isolated as its own section.
- **quote:** "the heart of James's concern seems to be the violent quarrels that are shaking the community… While we have presented the material in something of a chiastic pattern, we don't think a genuine chiasm is evident here… the call to repentance in 4:4-10 stands out in many ways as a critical section in the letter… We signal this central role by isolating the unit as a section in its own right."
- **locus:** L8–L10
- **passage:** Intro structure note

### C-R4-005
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo relates 3:1–12 both to 2:14–26 (Tasker: “words are also works”; cf. Matt. 12:37 on judgment by words) and to 1:26 / 1:19–20 (control of the tongue as a clear mark of true religion).
- **quote:** "the concern about \"words\" in this paragraph is loosely connected to the concern about \"works\" in 2:14-26; as Tasker puts it, \"words are also works.\"… this long section on the problem of the tongue picks up James's identification of the control of the tongue as one of the clearest examples of \"true religion\" (1:26; cf. 1:19-20)."
- **locus:** L22
- **passage:** 3:1–12 opening links

### C-R4-006
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo prefers the view that v. 1 uses teachers as a convenient jumping-off point for a general warning about the tongue, rather than directing the whole paragraph mainly to Christian leaders; v. 1 addresses those who might want to become teachers; 4:1 and 4:11 show sinful speech involves more than leaders.
- **quote:** "we prefer the former view: a concern about people wanting to teach leads James into a general warning about the tongue… Verse 1, after all, is directed not to Christian leaders, but to any Christian who might want to become a teacher. The general address to the readers in 4:1 and 4:11 certainly demonstrates that the problem of sinful, critical speech involved more than the leaders."
- **locus:** L24
- **passage:** 3:1 occasion / audience

### C-R4-007
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo outlines 3:1–12 in four stages: (1) vv. 1–2 teachers and difficulty of controlling the tongue; (2) vv. 3–6 power of the tongue (summarized 5a); (3) vv. 7–8 difficulty of control; (4) vv. 9–12 the tongue’s “doubleness” typical of sin in James.
- **quote:** "The paragraph unfolds in four stages. (1) In vv. 1-2… (2) The incredible power of the tongue is the theme of vv. 3-6… (3) Powerful as it is, the tongue is extremely difficult to keep under control (vv. 7-8). (4) Verses 9-12 end the passage on a note typical for James… the tongue reveals its evil nature by manifesting that \"doubleness\" which is so typical of sin."
- **locus:** L26
- **passage:** 3:1–12 structure

### C-R4-008
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: uncontrolled speech is frequent in secular moralists and OT/Jewish Wisdom (esp. Proverbs as key marker of godliness); James’s illustrations show a reasonably well-educated Jew who knows the OT thoroughly and is well acquainted with Hellenistic-Jewish culture, without requiring deep Greco-Roman philosophical training.
- **quote:** "The problem of uncontrolled speech is a frequent theme among secular moralists and in OT and Jewish Wisdom literature. Especially is this motif prominent in Proverbs… The picture of James that emerges is of a reasonably well-educated Jew who knows his OT thoroughly and who is well acquainted with Hellenistic-Jewish culture, language, and literature."
- **locus:** L28
- **passage:** Background of 3:1–12

### C-R4-009
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: early-church teachers (*didaskaloi*) roughly equivalent to the Jewish rabbi; they expounded the gospel from growing tradition (unlike prophets’ revelations); prestige plus low literacy/status mobility made the role attractive; too many sought it without moral (and perhaps intellectual) qualifications; unfit teachers may have fueled partisan spirit (3:13–18), quarreling (4:1), and critical speech (4:11).
- **quote:** "Teachers (didaskaloi) were prominent in the life of the early church… roughly the equivalent of the rabbi… Too many were seeking the status of teacher without the necessary moral (and perhaps also intellectual) qualifications. Perhaps, indeed, unfit teachers were a major cause of the bitter partisan spirit (cf. 3:13-18), quarreling (4:1), and unkind, critical speech (4:11)"
- **locus:** L32
- **passage:** 3:1 teachers

### C-R4-010
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo’s third reading of *krima* in 3:1: not merely “more severe condemnation” (KJV sense of *krima*) nor only neutral “stricter judgment,” but that teachers, whose ministry is speech—the hardest body-part to control—expose themselves to greater danger of judgment and will be scrutinized more carefully (cf. Luke 12:48; Mark 12:40).
- **quote:** "the logic of James's argument… suggests a third interpretation of the \"greater judgment\": teachers, because their ministry involves speech, the hardest of all parts of the body to control, expose themselves to greater danger of judgment… Teachers, because they bear so much responsibility for the spiritual welfare of those to whom they minister, will be scrutinized by the Lord more carefully than others."
- **locus:** L34–L36
- **passage:** 3:1 *krima* / stricter judgment

### C-R4-011
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: James does not discourage appropriately called and gifted people from teaching, but impresses the seriousness of the calling and warns against insincere or cavalier motives.
- **quote:** "Of course, James is not trying to talk people who have the appropriate call and the gift out of becoming teachers. But he does want to impress upon us the seriousness of this calling and to warn us about entering into the ministry with insincere or cavalier motivations."
- **locus:** L36
- **passage:** 3:1 pastoral application

### C-R4-012
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo links v. 2 to v. 1 with *gar*: teachers are more susceptible to judgment because they regularly engage in speech, the hardest activity to keep from sin; “we all stumble in many ways” (*polla*) favors variety of sins, not merely many mistakes; *ptaio* may suggest minor/inadvertent sin (cf. Sir. 19:16).
- **quote:** "Teachers are more susceptible to judgment than others because they regularly engage in that activity which is hardest to keep from sin - one's speech… James's argument requiring reference not to the number but to the variety of sins… it may suggest a minor or inadvertent sin."
- **locus:** L38
- **passage:** 3:2 stumble / logic with v. 1

### C-R4-013
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo: one never at fault in speech would be a “perfect” person able to bridle the whole body; *chalinagōgeō* “bridle” harks back to 1:26 and anticipates the bit metaphor of v. 3; closest parallel Philo, *Posterity* 88; theme is staple of Jewish Wisdom and Hellenistic moral exhortation.
- **quote:** "If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to keep his whole body in check… The word for keep in check here means, literally, \"bridle.\" The word both harks back to 1:26… and anticipates the metaphor of v. 3… But Philo provides the closest parallel"
- **locus:** L40
- **passage:** 3:2 perfect / bridle

### C-R4-014
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo on the bit and ship illustrations (3:3–4): small controls large; ship image adds the pilot’s *hormē* (will/impulse), setting up v. 5’s triad—guiding desire (steersman), means of control (rudder/tongue), that controlled (ship/body); horse/ship/fire imagery widespread (Philo, Plutarch, etc.), so James need not depend on any single source.
- **quote:** "James thus sets up the application that he will make of these images in v. 5, with all three key components in place: \"the guiding desire (the steersman), the means of control (the rudder), and that which is controlled (the ship), corresponding in turn to human desire, the tongue, and the body.\"… The point in citing these parallels is not to argue that James depends on any one of them directly."
- **locus:** L50–L58 (approx. cache mid-section on vv. 3–4)
- **passage:** 3:3–4 bit and ship

### C-R4-015
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: in 3:5a “tongue” first appears by metonymy for speech; *aucheō* “boasts” is here more neutral (legitimate claim to power) than the negative boasting of 4:16–17; 5b’s spark/forest shifts to destructiveness and introduces fire dominating 5b–6; *hēlikos* used for both “great” and “small”; “forest” (*hylē*, “wood”) may mean dry Palestinian brush more than rare forests.
- **quote:** "Here, however, it is used more neutrally: the tongue can legitimately make the claim to have considerable power… the point being illustrated shifts slightly, since the nuance of destructiveness is now added… the words \"great\" and \"small\" translate the same Greek word… James might then be referring not so much to a \"forest\"… but to the brush that covers so many Palestinian hills"
- **locus:** L60–L62
- **passage:** 3:5a–b boasts / spark

### C-R4-016
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: fire advances the argument—the tiny tongue not only has disproportionate power (bit/rudder) but potential for disaster (spark); OT Prov. 16:27 and Sir. 28:22 compare scoundrel speech / tongue to fire.
- **quote:** "not only does the tiny tongue - like the bit and the rudder - possess power all out of proportion to its size; it also has the potential to bring disaster - like the spark in a dry forest."
- **locus:** L64
- **passage:** 3:5b fire advance

### C-R4-017
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects *kosmos* as “adornment of evil” or Vulgate “sum/mass”; prefers fallen “world” / “unrighteous world” as in James’s other uses (1:27; 4:4); majority translation of 3:6: tongue is a fire; the tongue is appointed/makes itself among the members as the world of unrighteousness, staining the body and setting existence on fire.
- **quote:** "The most common meaning of kosmos in the NT is \"world,\" often with the nuance of the fallen, sinful world-system. This is the meaning the word has in its three other occurrences in James (1:27; 4:4)… \"And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is appointed among our members as the world of unrighteousness, staining the whole body, setting on fire the course of existence….\""
- **locus:** L70–L80
- **passage:** 3:6 *kosmos adikias* syntax

### C-R4-018
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo prefers middle sense of *kathistatai* (cf. 4:4 “makes oneself”): the tongue “appoints” itself as the unrighteous world—conduit of the world’s evil in us (Calvin: slender flesh contains whole world of iniquity); cf. Matt. 15:11, 18–19 on what comes from the mouth.
- **quote:** "James uses the same form of this verb in a similar construction in 4:4, where it is middle and has the meaning \"makes oneself.\"… the tongue, by virtue of being the most difficult of all parts of the body to control, becomes the conduit by which all the evil of the world around us comes to expression in us."
- **locus:** L80
- **passage:** 3:6 *kathistatai*

### C-R4-019
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: staining (*spilousa*) the whole person (*sōma* = whole being) destroys true religion’s demand to stay unstained (*aspilon*) by the world (1:27); “wheel of existence/origin” need not prove non-Palestinian authorship (contra Ropes); as widespread Hellenistic Jewish idiom for life’s ups and downs, NIV “whole course of life” is right; source of destructive power is *gehenna* (Valley of Hinnom)—only elsewhere in NT on Jesus’ lips—so Satan’s power fuels the tongue.
- **quote:** "By \"corrupting\" or \"staining\" (spilousa) the whole person, the tongue destroys \"true religion\"… The NIV translation the whole course of life therefore captures the sense… From hell, says James… James again betrays his connection to Jesus, since only in the teaching of Jesus do we find this word elsewhere in the NT (11 times). The power of Satan himself, the chief denizen of hell, gives to the tongue its great destructive potential."
- **locus:** L86
- **passage:** 3:6 stain / wheel / gehenna

### C-R4-020
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: James does not list speech-sins but would think of Proverbs types (chattering, lying, arrogant boasting, gossiping); rumors can be harder to stop than forest fire; childhood “sticks and stones” taunt reverses the truth.
- **quote:** "he undoubtedly would have thought of those sins of speech that are enumerated in Proverbs… Such a rumor can be harder to stop than any forest fire (v. 5)… Far easier to heal are the wounds caused by sticks and stones than the damage caused by words."
- **locus:** L88
- **passage:** 3:6 pastoral elaboration

### C-R4-021
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: 3:7–8 give evidence (*gar*) that the tongue is set on fire by hell—human inability to train it; fourfold animal list reflects Gen. 1:26 dominion; taming is rooted in image of God and mandate to subdue; present + perfect of “tame” mark ongoing process grounded in the creation state.
- **quote:** "The verses are formally introduced (note the for) as evidence that the tongue is, indeed, \"set on fire by hell\" (v. 6)… this fourfold division of the animal kingdom clearly reflects the Genesis creation account… Human ability to \"tame\" the animal world, suggests James, is inherent in the image of God and the divine mandate to \"subdue\" the world."
- **locus:** L90
- **passage:** 3:7 animals tamed

### C-R4-022
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects Augustine’s reading that “no one of men” leaves room for God to tame the tongue unto perfection in this life; Moo already denied attainable perfection at 1:4; ultimate taming is impossible, yet that should not dampen effort toward better control.
- **quote:** "We have answered this question in the negative (see our comments on 1:4). We therefore doubt that Augustine's interpretation is correct. James does, indeed, suggest that the ultimate taming of the tongue is impossible… The realization that perfection in something is unattainable should not dampen in the least our enthusiasm to become as good at it as possible."
- **locus:** L92
- **passage:** 3:8 no one can tame

### C-R4-023
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: tongue is a “restless evil, full of deadly poison”; *akatastaton* “restless” is the same word as for the double-minded man “unstable” in 1:8; cf. Prov. 26:28 LXX; Hermas *Mandate* 2.3 on slander as restless demon.
- **quote:** "it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison… The word \"restless\" translates the same word that James used in 1:8 to describe the \"double-minded man, unstable in all he does.\""
- **locus:** L94
- **passage:** 3:8 restless evil

### C-R4-024
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: 3:9–12 attribute to the tongue the “doubleness” James frequently deplores—epitomized by the double-minded man (1:8; 4:8); same tongue praises “our Lord and Father” and curses humans made in God’s likeness (Gen. 1:26; cf. Genesis Rabbah 24).
- **quote:** "James brings his critique of the tongue to a conclusion by attributing to it the \"doubleness\" that he so frequently deplores… And now, we find, they use the same tongue both to praise our Lord and Father and to curse men, who have been made in God's likeness."
- **locus:** L96–L98
- **passage:** 3:9 blessing and cursing

### C-R4-025
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: shift from “tongue” to “mouth” and “come out” (3:10) likely depends on Jesus (Matt. 15:11, 17–20; 12:37); what comes from the mouth is a spirituality barometer; Jewish parallels include T. Benjamin 6:5 (not talking from both sides of the mouth) and Sir. 5:14–6:1 (double-tongued).
- **quote:** "His shift in this verse to \"mouth\" and the language… of \"come out\" probably reflects his dependence once again on the teaching of Jesus… And nowhere does the tongue reveal its evil power more than in its doubleness… T. Benjamin 6:5: \"the good set of mind does not talk from both sides of its mouth\""
- **locus:** L100–L104
- **passage:** 3:10 same mouth

### C-R4-026
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: “this should not be” captures moral outrage; Spirit-transformed Christians should show heart-wholeness in consistent pure speech; springs/trees/salt-spring illustrations (3:11–12) show absurdity of mixed production; *pikros* “bitter” (not only “salt”) may echo OT/Jewish descriptions of wrong speech; one double and inconsistent toward God (*dipsychos*, 1:8; 4:8) will be double in speech.
- **quote:** "Christians who have been transformed by the Spirit of God should manifest the wholeness and purity of the heart in consistency and purity of speech… One who is double and inconsistent with regard to the things of God in his heart (dipsychos, 1:8 and 4:8) will be double and inconsistent in his speech."
- **locus:** L106–L116
- **passage:** 3:10–12 springs/trees → double-mindedness

### C-R4-027
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo cautions against pressing tree imagery into automatic moral perfectionism: “A man is after all not a tree” (Berkhof); only a renewed heart produces pure speech, and consistently (not perfectly) pure speech should be the product of the renewed heart.
- **quote:** "As theologian Hendrikus Berkhof trenchantly reminds us, \"A man is after all not a tree.\"… only a renewed heart can produce pure speech; and consistently (though not perfectly) pure speech is to be the product of the renewed heart."
- **locus:** L116 (end of 3:12)
- **passage:** 3:12 limits of plant imagery

### C-R4-028
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo argues against a sharp break between 3:13–18 and 4:1–3: *zēlos* envy of earthly wisdom (3:16) and *zēloō* “covet” (4:2) bind the paragraphs; James depends on a widespread Hellenistic-Jewish topos tracing social ills to jealousy (*zēlos*) and envy (*phthonos*); closest parallels in *Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs* (slander, violence, murder from jealousy; double-mindedness); direct dependence unlikely.
- **quote:** "James is especially concerned about the unrighteous and misguided \"zeal\" or \"envy\" (Gk. zelos) that people characterized by \"earthly\" wisdom are displaying (3:16); and it is this same envy (zeloo; translated \"covet\" in NIV) that is leading to bitter arguments in the community (4:2)… James depends in this section of his letter on a widespread Hellenistic-Jewish moral topos… that traced social ills back to jealousy (zelos) and envy (phthonos)."
- **locus:** L122 (after 4:1–3 NIV block; intro to 3:13–4:3 continuity)
- **passage:** Continuity 3:13–4:3 / envy topos

### C-R4-029
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: common thread of 3:13–18 and 4:1–3 is peace—false wisdom yields envy, selfishness, disorder; heavenly wisdom is especially “peace loving,” climaxing in peacemakers (v. 18); 4:1–3 absence of peace traces to envy and selfishness of 3:14; whole community in view, not only leaders (contra Martin-style teacher-only reading of 3:1–4:3).
- **quote:** "The common thread running through both paragraphs is peace… The absence of peace, on the other hand, is obviously the main issue in 4:1-3… we have argued above that 3:1-12 is directed to the entire community; and we think it likely that 3:13-4:3 is also."
- **locus:** L124–L128
- **passage:** Peace thread; audience of 3:13–4:3

### C-R4-030
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo: “Who is wise and understanding among you?” is not limited to teachers—*sophos*/*epistēmōn* not regular teacher titles; LXX applies the pair to leaders and to all Israel; James already said all should seek wisdom (1:5); true wisdom shown by good life and deeds in humility that comes from wisdom (*prautēs*), not by doctrinal/parse prowess; humility from recognizing creaturely position before God (elaborated 4:7).
- **quote:** "neither \"wise\" (sophos) nor \"understanding\" (epistemon) is regularly used as a title for the teacher… James assesses these people's claim to wisdom not in theological terms… but in practical terms: Let him show it by his good life, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom… true wisdom produces good works and true wisdom produces humility."
- **locus:** L130–L132
- **passage:** 3:13 wise and understanding

### C-R4-031
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: testing wisdom by life fits OT wisdom (Prov. 1:7; 2:9, 20); contrasts Greek intellectual/mystery wisdom sometimes at expense of morals (cf. Corinth); James’s rebuke targets failure to live out wisdom’s implications more than a defined false theory of wisdom; James’s conception of wisdom remains relatively undeveloped conceptually.
- **quote:** "James's insistence that wisdom is to be tested by the kind of life one lives is in keeping with the idea of wisdom in the OT… His rebuke of false wisdom is not so much directed against a particular view of wisdom as against a failure of people to live out in the ways they should the implications of wisdom."
- **locus:** L134
- **passage:** 3:13 biblical vs Greek wisdom

### C-R4-032
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: harboring bitter envy (*zēlos*, here negative “envy”) and selfish ambition (*eritheia*—Aristotle’s partisan political zeal) denies a claim to wisdom because they contradict humility; do not boast (*katakauchaomai*) or deny the truth.
- **quote:** "if a person harbors bitter envy and selfish ambition in the heart, that person is, in effect, living a lie… The only attested pre-NT occurrence of the word comes in Aristotle, who uses it to describe the narrow partisan zeal of factional, greedy politicians… Some who pride themselves on their wisdom and understanding are displaying a jealous, bitter partisanship that is the antithesis of the humility produced by true wisdom."
- **locus:** L136–L140
- **passage:** 3:14 envy and selfish ambition

### C-R4-033
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: such “wisdom” (NIV quotes = phantom) does not come down from above/heaven (cf. 1:17 good gifts); it is earthly (earthbound, ignoring God’s realm), unspiritual (*psychikos*), of the devil/demonic.
- **quote:** "Such \"wisdom\" does not come down from heaven… It is earthly, unspiritual, of the devil… \"earthbound\" is a good rendering."
- **locus:** L142–L144
- **passage:** 3:15 earthly / unspiritual / demonic

### C-R4-034
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: *gar* in 3:16—effects justify the harsh verdict: where envy and selfish ambition are, there is disorder (*akatastasia*, related to unstable/restless of 1:8 and 3:8) and every evil practice.
- **quote:** "When people hold such attitudes, the result can only be disorder and every evil practice. The Greek word translated \"disorder\" (akatastasia) is another form of a word that James has used in 1:8 and 3:8 to describe the \"double-minded\" person and the \"double-speaking\" tongue."
- **locus:** L146
- **passage:** 3:16 disorder

### C-R4-035
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo: heavenly wisdom is known by what it *does*—practical orientation like true faith (2:14–26); resemblance to Gal. 5:22–23 fruit of the Spirit is real in effect (humility, peaceableness, uprightness) but Moo cautions against equating James’s wisdom with Paul’s Spirit—James writes before familiarity with Pauline theology; OT/Jewish profile attributes godly character to wisdom; Paul attributes it to the Spirit under new-covenant development.
- **quote:** "Like true faith (2:14-26), true wisdom is identified by the quality of life that it produces… In a general sense, what Paul claims that the Spirit produces, James claims true wisdom produces… equivalence in effect between wisdom in James and the Spirit in Paul does not mean equivalence in the two entities themselves."
- **locus:** L148
- **passage:** 3:17 wisdom and Spirit analogy

### C-R4-036
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: first/preeminent fruit is purity (*hagnos*); seven following qualities are dimensions of purity, literarily grouped: (1) *eirēnikē, epieikēs, eupeithēs* (peace-loving, considerate, “easily persuaded”/willing deference); (2) full of mercy and good fruit; (3) *adiakritos, anypokritos*. Peace-loving heads the specific virtues and anticipates 4:1–2 dissensions.
- **quote:** "The first, and preeminent, attribute that wisdom produces is purity… The seven qualities that follow in the list are specific dimensions of this overall purity… \"Peace loving\" is especially important, coming at the head of the list of specific virtues and being picked up for further emphasis in v. 18."
- **locus:** L150–L152
- **passage:** 3:17 list structure

### C-R4-037
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: *eupeithēs* is not weak gullibility but willing deference when unalterable theological/moral principles are not at stake; mercy (*eleos*) = neighbor-love in action (2:8–13), coupled with good fruit as wisdom’s necessary products (like faith).
- **quote:** "What is meant is not a weak, credulous gullibility, but a willing deference to others when unalterable theological or moral principles are not involved… James provides his own definition of \"mercy\": love for the neighbor that shows itself in action (2:8-13)."
- **locus:** L152–L154
- **passage:** 3:17 submissive / mercy

### C-R4-038
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo leans *adiakritos* toward undivided loyalty / “not double” (fits *diakrinō* in 1:6; 2:4 and anti–double-minded plea near 4:8) more than only “impartial,” though both have support; pairs with *anypokritos* “sincere / not play-acting”—stable, transparent counselor.
- **quote:** "he uses the verb diakrino to mean \"be divided\" in 1:6 and 2:4; and one of James's central pleas is for \"undivided\" loyalty to God - not least in this general context (see \"double-minded\" in 4:7 [sic 4:8])… The person characterized by wisdom from heaven will be stable, trustworthy, transparent"
- **locus:** L156
- **passage:** 3:17 *adiakritos* / *anypokritos*

### C-R4-039
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo slightly prefers NIV sense of 3:18: peacemakers who sow in peace raise a harvest of righteousness (what peacemakers produce) over NRSV’s “for those who make peace,” because it better contrasts demonic wisdom’s evil practices (v. 16); “fruit of righteousness” = fruit that is righteousness (epexegetic; common in LXX), conduct pleasing to God (as in 1:20), including v. 17 virtues; cf. Matt. 5:9.
- **quote:** "we slightly incline toward the NIV interpretation… Righteousness in Jas. 1:20 meant that conduct which is pleasing to God, and this is the \"fruit\" intended here also. It includes all the virtues listed in v. 17 and is the opposite… of \"every evil practice\" (v. 16)."
- **locus:** L158–L160 (3:18 section)
- **passage:** 3:18 harvest of righteousness

### C-R4-040
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: 4:1 does not introduce a wholly new topic but shifts focus within the peace/envy discussion; 3:13–18 prepares for rebuking quarreling because James focuses on wisdom’s peace-producing fruit, not wisdom per se.
- **quote:** "The beginning of chap. 4, then, does not introduce a new topic, but a shift of focus within discussion of the same topic… He is not really interested in talking about wisdom per se, but in that fruit of wisdom which brings order and peace to the church."
- **locus:** L171
- **passage:** 4:1 continuity with 3:13–18

### C-R4-041
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo rejects taking *polemoi*/*machai* primarily as literal community warfare/murder (contra Martin’s Zealot background possibility): *machai* in LXX/NT often verbal quarrels; *polemos* can be metaphorical (e.g. Pss. Sol. 12:3 slander kindles strife); metaphorical “fights/quarrels” fit the tongue theme (3:1–12; 4:11–12; 5:9); James’s concern is selfish spirit and bitterness more than adjudicating issues.
- **quote:** "We think that this metaphorical meaning is likely here, despite the presence of the word \"kill\" in v. 2… disputes are almost always accompanied by harsh words, criticism, and slander - the misuse of the tongue that James castigates… his concern was more with the selfish spirit and bitterness of the quarrels than with the rights and wrongs of the various viewpoints."
- **locus:** L173–L177
- **passage:** 4:1 fights and quarrels

### C-R4-042
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: source of quarrels is *hēdonai*—pleasures with sinful self-indulgent connotation (NT always negative)—battling “in your members,” more likely parts of the individual body (cf. 1 Pet. 2:11) than members of the church; James would add jealousy and selfish ambition to lists like 4 Macc. 1:25–26.
- **quote:** "Desires translates the Greek word hedone, which means simply \"pleasure,\" but often with the connotation of a sinful, self-indulgent pleasure… The former is a bit more likely when we consider the close parallel to this language in 1 Pet. 2:11"
- **locus:** L179
- **passage:** 4:1 *hēdonai* / members

### C-R4-043
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc, wisdom-literature]
- **claim:** Moo prefers two-clause punctuation of 4:2 (NRSV etc.): frustrated desire → murder; coveting without obtaining → disputes/conflicts—paralleling Hellenistic moral tradition where envy/jealousy lead to quarrels, murder, wars (T. Simeon on envy; Epictetus; NT examples of *phthonos*/*zēlos*).
- **quote:** "In favor of the second punctuation is especially the parallelism that is created… This fits better into the context, since James has been at pains to show that disorder and evil in the community stem from \"bitter envy and selfish ambition\" (3:14-16)… According to this tradition, \"envy\" (phthonos) and \"jealousy\" (zelos…) inevitably lead to hostile acts"
- **locus:** L181–L185
- **passage:** 4:2 structure / envy tradition

### C-R4-044
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo on “you kill” (*phoneuete*): not actual intra-church murder (strains credulity; Zealot violence not typically against fellow religionists); rejects Erasmus’s emendation *phthoneite*; not merely spiritualized Matt. 5:21–26 murderous anger without contextual prep; best: literal sense as hypothetical end-product of unchecked envy—warning of where covetous zeal may lead while fightings are already present.
- **quote:** "It strains credulity to suppose that James would pass so quickly over so serious a matter within the community… Perhaps, then, the best alternative is to take \"you kill\" in its normal, literal, sense, but as a hypothetical eventuality rather than as an actual occurrence… James is warning his readers about just where their envious desires might lead them if not checked in time."
- **locus:** L187
- **passage:** 4:2 phoneuete

### C-R4-045
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo finds a chiasm in 4:1–2a (fights ← wrong desires ← frustrated desire → quarrels); analysis of conflict: verbal, private violence, or national conflict all trace to wrongful lust to want more / envy of others’ position or possessions.
- **quote:** "We therefore have something of a chiasm in vv. 1-2a… Verbal argument, private violence, or national conflict - the cause of them all can be traced back to the wrongful lust to want more than we have, to be envious of and covet what others have, whether it be their position or their possessions."
- **locus:** L189
- **passage:** 4:1–2a chiasm / analysis of conflict

### C-R4-046
- **topic_tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **claim:** Moo: “you do not have, because you do not ask God” (4:2c) and “when you ask… wrong motives… pleasures” (4:3)—context suggests they want wisdom/recognition as leaders (3:1; 3:13) but fail to ask as 1:5 commands; when they ask, motive is to spend freely (*dapanaō*, negative as prodigal Luke 15:14) on *hēdonai*; Jesus’ ask-promise (Matt. 7:7) assumes asking ordered to God’s name/kingdom/will (Matt. 6:9–10), not warlike pleasures (Hort).
- **quote:** "the context suggests an answer: the kind of wisdom that will enable them to gain recognition as leaders in the community… You do not have, because you do not ask God… you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may spend what you get on your pleasures… petitions to Him which have no better end in view are not prayers."
- **locus:** L191–L195
- **passage:** 4:2c–3 ask / wrong motives
